claims.text: High-temperature oxidation resistance and sustained material integrity in multiprincipal-element alloys are governed by formation of a continuous, adherent oxide scale enriched in selective refractory oxide-forming elements such as Al and Cr.
The protective oxide scale slows oxygen ingress by acting as a kinetic barrier.
Protective-scale formation is critically determined by alloy composition and high-temperature phase stability.
The relevant continuous, dense surface oxide consists primarily of Al2O3 and/or Cr2O3.
A sufficient concentration of oxide-forming elements promotes early and uniform nucleation of a protective oxide layer.
The resulting protective oxide layer adheres strongly to the alloy substrate.
A coherent protective oxide layer slows diffusion of oxygen and metal ions.
Alloys deficient in Al and Cr fail to form a coherent oxide scale.
Failure to form a coherent oxide scale leads to accelerated oxidation.
Failure to form a coherent oxide scale promotes spallation during thermal cycling.
Higher optimized Al and/or Cr levels will produce a more robust protective oxide scale than lower Al/Cr levels.
Higher optimized Al and/or Cr levels will lower oxidation rates relative to a lower-Al/Cr baseline.
Higher optimized Al and/or Cr levels will enhance structural integrity over time relative to a lower-Al/Cr baseline.
A lower-Al/Cr control alloy is expected to exhibit higher oxidation rates and a less coherent oxide layer under otherwise identical conditions.
The proposed governing behavior is expected to hold from 800 to 1100 °C in air or oxygen-rich atmospheres.
At temperatures significantly outside 800–1100 °C or in non-oxidizing atmospheres, other degradation mechanisms may dominate.
Threshold compositions for optimal oxide-scale formation may depend on secondary phases, microstructural heterogeneity, and interactions among principal elements.
